question: How much money does PM-KISAN give an eligible farmer family each year, and how is it paid out?
gold_answer: Rs 6,000 per year, paid in three installments of Rs 2,000 each, one every four months (April-July, August-November, December-March), directly into the beneficiary's bank account through DBT.
answer: PM-KISAN gives an eligible farmer family an amount of Rs.6000/- per year. This amount is released in three installments of Rs.2000/- each every 4-month/trimester, i.e., April-July, August-November, and December-March [pmkisan_operational_guidelines_2020.pdf, Page 9].

question: How does PM-KISAN define a landholder farmer's family?
gold_answer: A family comprising husband, wife and minor children who own cultivable land as per the land records of the concerned State/UT.
answer: A landholder farmer's family is defined as "a family comprising of husband, wife and minor children who owns cultivable land as per land records of the concerned State/UT". The existing land-ownership system will be used for identification of beneficiaries for calculation of benefit. [pmkisan_operational_guidelines_2020.pdf, Page 1]

question: What is the cut-off date used to decide eligibility under PM-KISAN?
gold_answer: 01.02.2019 (1 February 2019). No later changes count for eligibility for the next 5 years, except when ownership transfers because of the landowner's death.
answer: The cut-off date for determination of eligibility of beneficiaries under the scheme shall be 01.02.2019 and no changes thereafter shall be considered for eligibility of benefit under the scheme for next 5 years. However, this date is not applicable when transfer of ownership of cultivable land takes place on account of succession due to death. [pmkisan_operational_guidelines_2020.pdf, Page 3]

question: Is a retired government pensioner who gets Rs 12,000 a month eligible for PM-KISAN?
gold_answer: No. Retired pensioners whose monthly pension is Rs 10,000 or more are excluded, except former Multi Tasking Staff/Class IV/Group D employees.
answer: Not found in the documents

question: A family sells all its cultivable land to another farmer by sale deed in 2021. What happens to the PM-KISAN eligibility of the buyer and the seller?
gold_answer: The buyer is not eligible because he or she was not the land owner on 01.02.2019. The seller also becomes ineligible if the seller's family has no cultivable land after the transfer.
answer:
According to the provided context, in cases of cultivable land transferred to other persons through Sale Deed, Partition Deed, Gift Deed, etc., the transferee will not be eligible under the Scheme as he/she was not the land owner as on 01.02.2019. However, in such cases, even the transferor of the land will become ineligible if the family of the transferor does not have any cultivable land subsequent to such a transfer.

Therefore, in the scenario described:

- The buyer (transferee) will not be eligible for PM-KISAN benefits.
- The seller (transferor) will lose eligibility if the seller's family no longer has any cultivable land after the transfer.

question: Which states were exempted from the Aadhaar requirement under PM-KISAN, and until when?
gold_answer: Assam, Meghalaya and Jammu & Kashmir, until 31.3.2021.
answer: The states exempted from the Aadhaar requirement under PM-KISAN were Assam, Meghalaya, and Jammu & Kashmir. This exemption was valid until 31.3.2021. [pmkisan_operational_guidelines_2020.pdf, Page 6]

question: What interest rate do farmers pay on short-term KCC loans in 2025-26 under the interest subvention scheme, and what is the effective rate if they repay on time?
gold_answer: 7% per annum. With the additional 3% prompt repayment incentive, farmers who repay on time effectively pay 4% per annum.
answer: Farmers will pay a lending rate of 7% on short-term KCC loans in 2025-26. If they repay on time, from the date of disbursement/drawal/renewal of the loan/s up to the actual date of repayment/tenure/due date or up to the due date fixed by the banks for repayment of such loan/s, whichever is earlier, they will receive an additional interest subvention of 3% per annum. Therefore, the effective rate for farmers who repay on time would be 4% per annum.

question: For how long after harvest can small and marginal farmers keep getting interest subvention, and under what condition?
gold_answer: Up to six months after harvest, against negotiable warehouse receipts for produce stored in WDRA-accredited warehouses.
answer:
For how long after harvest can small and marginal farmers keep getting interest subvention, and under what condition?

Small and marginal farmers can get interest subvention for a further period of up to six months post the harvest of the crop against negotiable warehouse receipts on the produce stored in warehouses accredited with Warehousing Development Regulatory Authority (WDRA), at the same rate as applicable to the crop loan from the date of pledge. [1, Page 2]

question: What is the maximum premium a farmer pays under PMFBY for Kharif food grain and oilseed crops, for Rabi food grain and oilseed crops, and for annual commercial or horticultural crops?
gold_answer: 2.0% of sum insured for Kharif food grain and oilseeds, 1.5% for Rabi food grain and oilseeds, and 5% for annual commercial/horticultural crops, in each case or the actuarial rate, whichever is less.
answer:
For Kharif food grain and oilseed crops, the maximum premium a farmer pays under PMFBY is 2.0% of the sum insured or actuarial rate, whichever is less [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 47].

For Rabi food grain and oilseed crops, the maximum premium a farmer pays under PMFBY is 1.5% of the sum insured or actuarial rate, whichever is less [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 47].

For annual commercial or horticultural crops, the maximum premium a farmer pays under PMFBY is 5% of the sum insured or actuarial rate, whichever is less [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 47].

question: How is the normal PMFBY premium subsidy shared between the Centre and the States?
gold_answer: Equally, 50:50, in all States/UTs except the Himalayan and North Eastern Region States/UTs, where the ratio is 90:10.
answer: The normal PMFBY premium subsidy is shared equally in a 50:50 ratio by the Centre and State/UTs in all State/UTs except Himalayan & North Eastern Region (NER) State/UTs, where the subsidy sharing pattern between the Centre and State/UTs is in the 90:10 ratio.

question: Which farmers are eligible for PMFBY coverage, and what must they submit?
gold_answer: All farmers, including sharecroppers and tenant farmers, growing notified crops in notified areas, provided they have insurable interest in the crop and land. They must submit land or tenancy documents, their Aadhaar number, and a declaration about the crop sown or intended to be sown.
answer: Not found in the documents

question: How can a loanee farmer opt out of PMFBY, and by when?
gold_answer: By submitting a declaration to the loan-sanctioning bank branch at least seven days before the cut-off date for enrolment. Farmers who do not submit it are covered automatically.
answer: A loanee farmer can opt out of PMFBY by submitting a declaration to their respective bank branch. This must be done at least seven days prior to the cut-off date for enrolment of farmers for the respective season. Not found in the documents

question: What are the normal latest cut-off dates for enrolment under PMFBY for Kharif, Rabi and summer crops?
gold_answer: Normally not beyond 15 July for Kharif, 15 December for Rabi and 15 February for summer seasons.
answer:
The normal latest cut-off dates for enrolment under PMFBY are:
- For Kharif crops: 15th July of the current year
- For Rabi crops: 15th December of the current year
- For Summer crops: 15th February of the following year

These dates are mentioned in [1] pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf (Page 51).

question: Until when can a loanee farmer change the insured crop, and how must the request be made?
gold_answer: In writing to the bank branch up to 2 working days before the enrolment cut-off date, provided the new crop is also notified under the scheme.
answer: A loanee farmer can change the insured crop up to 2 working days before the cut-off date for enrolment. The request for changing the crop must be submitted in writing to the concerned bank branch. [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 66]

question: If an insurance company rejects a farmer's PMFBY application, within what time must the premium be refunded?
gold_answer: Within 45 days of the closure of the cut-off date for uploading data by banks, PACS and other channels. Otherwise the insurer must accept the application and pay claims as normal.
answer: If an insurance company rejects a farmer's PMFBY application, the premium must be refunded back to the farmer's bank account within 45 days of the closure of the cut-off date for uploading of data by Banks, PACS, CSC-VLEs, other authorized agencies/entities, BCs, Insurance Intermediaries, etc. [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 65]

question: Within how many hours must a farmer report localized crop damage such as hailstorm, and through which channels?
gold_answer: Within 72 hours, directly through the Crop Insurance App or the toll-free Krishi Rakshak Portal & Helpline number 14447. Intimation can also be forwarded through the bank branch or local agriculture or district officials.
answer:
A farmer must report localized crop damage such as a hailstorm within 72 hours. Reporting can be done through the following channels:

- Directly through the "Crop Insurance App"
- On the dedicated centralized toll-free number of Krishi Rakshak Portal & Helpline (14447)
- Through the concerned bank branch
- Through local agriculture department Government/district officials

The first mode of intimation should be either the "Crop Insurance App" or the centralized Toll-Free Number (KRPH) for this purpose.

question: A farmer's crop has a sum insured of Rs 30,000, 100% of the insured area is affected by hailstorm, and the estimated crop loss in the affected area is 80%. What localized calamity claim is payable?
answer: Claims payable = Rs. 30,000 x 100% x 80% = Rs. 24,000/-.

question: When is the prevented sowing cover triggered under PMFBY, and how much is paid?
gold_answer: When widespread eligible risks leave more than 75% of the normal sown area of the crop in the notified insurance unit unsown or failed to germinate. The payout is 25% of the gross total sum insured and the coverage then terminates.
answer: The prevented sowing cover under PMFBY is triggered when more than 75% of the normal sown area for a notified crop in an Insurance Unit (IU) experiences unsown or prevented sowing/germination failure during the sowing period due to widespread eligible risks, as per the crop calendar notified by the State/UT government. The payment for prevented sowing is 25% of the sum insured, which for a sum insured of Rs. 20,000 works out to Rs. 5,000. [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 92]

question: In the prevented sowing illustration, groundnut has a sum insured of Rs 20,000 per hectare and 80% of the area in an insurance unit could not be sown. How much is paid per hectare?
gold_answer: Rs 5,000, which is 25% of the Rs 20,000 sum insured.
answer: Not found in the documents

question: When can on-account payment for mid-season adversity be given, and how much is it?
gold_answer: When the expected yield of the affected crop in the notified insurance unit is less than 50% of normal yield. The amount payable is 25% of the likely claims, later adjusted against the final yield-based claim.
answer:
On-account payment for mid-season adversity can be given if the assessed loss of the affected crop is more than 50% of the normal crop yield for the Notified Insurance Unit. The on-account payment would be payable within 30 days from the date of the invocation of mid-term adversity. The amount of on-account payment is calculated as follows:

\[ \text{On-Account Payment} = \left( \frac{\text{Threshold Yield} - \text{Estimated Yield}}{\text{Threshold Yield}} \right) \times \text{Sum Insured} \times 25\% \]

Not found in the documents

question: How long after harvest does PMFBY cover post-harvest losses, and for which perils?
gold_answer: Up to a maximum of two weeks (14 days) from harvesting, for crops left in the field in cut-and-spread or bundled condition to dry, against hailstorm, cyclone, cyclonic rains and unseasonal rains.
answer: PMFBY covers post-harvest losses for crops that have been cut and are lying on the field, provided they have been notified for post-harvest cover and need to be kept on the field for drying up to a maximum of 14 days from harvest. The coverage applies to perils such as hailstorms, cyclones, cyclonic rains, and unseasonal rains, which must occur within 15 days of the onset of harvest and are supported by information from sources like WINDS, IMD, local media, and agriculture/revenue departments. Notified farmers who have paid the premium before the occurrence of the insured peril can claim for post-harvest losses within 72 hours of the occurrence of the peril.

question: From when does the wild animal attack add-on cover apply during the crop season?
gold_answer: From 30 days after sowing until harvesting. The State/UT must also notify the coverage duration.

question: Under the wild animal add-on cover, when is indemnity payable?
gold_answer: Only when the area affected by notified wild animals is more than 25% of the individual insured land parcel and the affected crop has less than 25% chance of revival till harvest.
answer: Under the wild animal add-on cover, indemnity is payable only when the area affected by notified wild animals is more than 25% of the individual insured land parcel, and the affected notified crop has less than 25% chances of crop revival till harvest. [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 171]

question: In the wild animal add-on illustration, sum insured is Rs 1,00,000, yield-based claim is Rs 40,000, crop loss from wild animals is Rs 70,000 and indemnity level is 80%. What are the total admissible claims and who pays what?
gold_answer: Total admissible claim is Rs 56,000 (80% of 70,000). PMFBY pays Rs 40,000 and the add-on cover (insurance company or corpus fund) pays the remaining Rs 16,000.
answer:
Total admissible claims to the farmers = Rs. 56,000
Liability of claims met through PMFBY (Insurance Company) = Rs. 40,000
Liability on Add-on Cover (Insurance Company or Corpus Fund) = Rs. 16,000

question: Within how many days must the Tehsil/Taluka grievance officer act on a farmer's grievance, and where can the farmer appeal?
gold_answer: Within 7 days of receiving the grievance. If dissatisfied, the farmer can appeal to the Appellate Committee (District Level Grievance Redressal Committee) headed by the District Magistrate/Collector, which disposes of the matter within 15 days.
answer: Within 7 days from the receipt of the grievance, the Tehsil/Taluk level grievance redressal Officer shall take suitable action as per the provisions of these guidelines. If the farmer is dissatisfied, the matter may be brought before the Appellate Committee (AC) constituted viz. District Level Grievance Redressal Committee (DGRC) [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 134].

question: If the average of the best five years of yield is 3,760 kg/ha, what is the threshold yield at an 80% indemnity level?
answer: The threshold yield at an 80% indemnity level would be 3,008 kg/ha. This is calculated by taking 80% of the average of the best five years of yield, which is 3,760 kg/ha (as given in the context). Therefore, 80% of 3,760 kg/ha is 3,008 kg/ha. [pmfby_operational_guidelines_2023.pdf, Page 88]

question: By how much can the notified sum insured change from one year to the next within a PMFBY contract period?

question: How do PM-KISAN and the KCC interest subvention scheme each use Aadhaar?
gold_answer: PM-KISAN: Aadhaar is collected for all beneficiaries and payments from the December 2019-March 2020 trimester onwards are made only on an Aadhaar-seeded database (Assam, Meghalaya and Jammu & Kashmir were exempted until 31.3.2021). KCC interest subvention 2025-26: Aadhaar seeding and authentication are mandatory and lending institutions must complete e-KYC for every farmer.
answer:
PM-KISAN uses Aadhaar for collecting the Aadhaar number of all beneficiaries for transferring the financial benefits. The financial benefit of Rs.6000 per year is released in three installments of Rs.2000 each every 4-month/trimester, and payment of all installments from December 2019 onwards is done on the basis of Aadhaar-seeded data base. However, states like Assam, Meghalaya, and Jammu & Kashmir were exempted from this requirement till 31.3.2021.

For KCC interest subvention, Aadhaar seeding and authentication are mandatory for availing benefits under the scheme. All lending institutions must ensure that e-KYC is completed for every farmer to enable seamless access to scheme benefits. [kcc_interest_subvention_2025_26.pdf, Page 2]
